newsitem.title: FRANCE: France to cut deficit to 3 pct of GDP, debt 58 pct.
newsitem.headline: France to cut deficit to 3 pct of GDP, debt 58 pct.

text.p: France's 1997 budget will cut the total public deficit to 3.0 percent of gross domestic product while the debt to GDP ratio will be 58 percent next year, the government said in a statement.
In documents detailing the 1997 budget, it said France would show a primary surplus, excluding debt service charges, next year for the first time since 1991.

The government pledged to continue spending curbs, aimed at reducing the total public deficit to below two percent of GDP in 2001. The tax burden will remain steady at 45.5 percent of gross domestic product next year after 45.6 percent in 1996.
The government said in a statement that its budget plans would ensure that France would meet all Maastricht treaty standards in 1997.

"The effort to control public spending will be continued beyond 1997, which will allow us to reduce long-term the deficit/GDP ratio below three percent while also reducing the tax burden," the statement said.
"Our aim is to reduce the deficit to less than two percent of GDP in 2001, so that it can be maintained at this level as was the case until the end of the 1970s," Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said.
The government repeated that it expected to meet its target of limiting the deficit/GDP ratio to four percent this year, despite an expected 15 billion franc shortfall in tax revenues.
It would limit the central government budget deficit to 288 billion francs this year as planned, thanks to a freezing of 20 billion francs in spending plans at the start of the year.
Next year, the reduction in the deficit would include a 37.5 billion franc transfer from France Telecom to the state to cover some pension liabilities.

Welfare debt repayment fund CADES would show an accounting surplus of around 12 billion francs compared to six billion this year. The 1997 accounts include all revenues raised by CADES from a new tax introduced earlier this year but include on the spending side only interest payments, rather than capital repayments on the welfare debt.
A bill on reforming financing for the social security system due shortly would aim to reduce its deficit to 30 billion francs in 1997.
"For the first time since 1991, the primary surplus of central government authorities will be positive in 1997," the statement said.
"As a result there will be slower growth in the debt/GDP ratio. This will be around 58 percent of GDP in 1997, after 56 percent in 1996, and 53 percent in 1995.
"Thanks to the continued efforts to reduce public deficits, this ratio should gradually stabilise below the ceiling of 60 percent of GDP in the course of the next few years," the statement said.
